svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 2. Three providers tested by reality, and what happened next
svg.desc: Three case studies. One provider claimed to keep no logs, supplied connection records to investigators in 2017, then commissioned an independent review in 2019 and a second in 2021 that permitted unannounced checks. A second provider supplied connection records in 2016 while under a previous owner, and has since changed hands twice, so the company that logged is not the company operating today. A third had its offices searched in 2023 by police intending to seize customer data, and had nothing to give. A band below argues that a permanent avoid list based on a single incident discards the most informative part of each story, which is what the provider did afterwards.
svg.text: Figure 2: What Providers Did After Being Tested
Standard guidance keeps a permanent avoid list. The incident is the least informative part of each of these stories.

g.text: 2017: it supplied records
A provider whose policy said it kept no logs
supplied connection records that helped
identify a suspect in a stalking case.
It later said its policy had meant browsing
activity rather than connection metadata.
2019 and 2021: it submitted to review
An independent review in 2019, and a second
in 2021 with a firm permitted to check
without prior notice.
Unannounced checking is a stronger regime
than most providers submit to, including
several on the recommended list.
2016: it supplied records
Another provider advertising no logging
supplied connection records to investigators.
And then it changed hands. Twice.
The company that kept those records is not
the company operating the service today,
and the current owner is a different
business with different people.
So what is the incident evidence of?
Something about the brand's history, and
very little about the operation you would
be buying from now. Ownership cuts both
ways, which nobody says.
2023: the police arrived
Officers executed a search warrant at a
provider's offices intending to seize
computers holding customer data.
The data did not exist. They left
without taking anything.
This is the strongest evidence available
about any provider, and it is rare because
somebody has to come looking first.
Notice that this happened in a country the
standard jurisdiction list tells you to
avoid, which is Section 4's argument in
one sentence.

svg.text: Why "caught once, avoid forever" is a lazy rule

g.text: It discards the informative half. What a provider does after an incident tells you about its current management. The incident tells you about a policy in 2016 or 2017.
It rewards never being tested. A provider nobody has ever come looking for sits above one that was tested and responded, purely because there is nothing on its record.
And it ignores ownership changes, which the same guidance treats as decisive when a company it dislikes buys a brand, and forgets when the ownership moves the other way.
None of which means the incidents do not matter. They do. They are one input, dated, alongside what came after.

svg.text: The distinction these incidents actually turned on, and it is worth carrying away
In both cases the provider supplied connection records rather than browsing history, and in both cases its marketing had said "no logs" without distinguishing the two.
A policy that does not name the categories separately is not a policy. It is a phrase, and Section 3 is about reading past it.
Judge a provider on its current architecture, its current ownership, and the most recent time anybody checked.
A list of villains from a decade ago is easier to write and tells the reader almost nothing about what to buy today.
